title: From the cow path to evacuation
summary: The line of work from Bellman's and Beck's linear search problem to group search with faulty robots, evacuation of disks and polygons, priority evacuation, and patrolling by robots with distinct speeds.

sections.heading: Linear search and the cow path
sections.body:
Kupavskii and Welzl open their paper with the original question, posed by Bellman in 1963 and studied by Beck, in Beck's words: "A man in an automobile searches for another man who is located at some point of a certain road. [...] How does he search so as to minimize the expected distance traveled?" [Kupavskii2018Lower] [Beck1964Linear]. In that version the searcher knows the distribution of the target. Beck and Newman showed, as reported by [Kupavskii2018Lower], that without knowledge of the distribution the distance cannot be smaller than 9 times the expected distance to the target.

Computer scientists rediscovered the problem as the cow-path problem: a cow at an infinite fence must find the gate, and optimality is the worst-case ratio between the distance travelled and the distance to the gate [Kupavskii2018Lower]. Doubling the turning point gives ratio 9 on the line, which is optimal; on $m$ rays, turning distances that grow by the factor $m/(m-1)$ give the optimal ratio $1+2m^m/(m-1)^{m-1}$ [BaezaYates1993Searching]; randomization lowers the line to about 4.59 [Kao1996Randomized]. Searching, Czyzowicz et al. note, "is central to many areas of computer science including data structures, computational geometry, and artificial intelligence" [Czyzowicz2021Byzantine].

sections.heading: Groups, faults and speeds
sections.body:
Czyzowicz et al. proposed parallel versions of the cow path in which $k$ robots search the line and up to $f$ of them are faulty [Kupavskii2018Lower]. A crash-faulty robot passes the target without detecting it [Czyzowicz2019FaultyLine]; a Byzantine robot may also stay silent or announce a target that is not there [Czyzowicz2021Byzantine]. For crash faults the optimal ratio is known exactly: proportional schedules [Czyzowicz2019FaultyLine] are optimal, as Kupavskii and Welzl proved [Kupavskii2018Lower]. For Byzantine faults it is not; already three robots with one liar are open [Czyzowicz2021Byzantine] [Kupavskii2018Lower].

The measure also changed. Bampas et al. compare search, where cost is "the time when the first searcher arrives", with rendezvous, where it is the time when "the last involved robot reaches the meeting point", and study two robots with different speeds that must both reach the target [Bampas2019Speeds]. They find optimal strategies for every speed ratio with communication by meeting, and show that wireless communication helps only up to a certain speed ratio [Bampas2019Speeds].

sections.heading: Evacuation: waiting for the last robot
sections.body:
Czyzowicz et al. posed evacuation: $k$ robots start at the centre of a unit disk and must all leave through an exit at an unknown point of the boundary; the cost is the worst-case time until the last robot is out [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. They compare it with the lost-at-sea and cow-path problems and with plane search, and cite Chrobak et al. for the observation that evacuation of uniform agents on a line "is as hard as the cow-path problem" [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating] [Chrobak2015GroupSearch]. Two communication models were introduced: wireless, in which a robot that finds the exit tells everyone at once, and face-to-face (local), in which robots exchange information only when they meet [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating].

For two wireless robots the answer is exactly $1+2\pi/3+\sqrt3 \approx 4.826$ [Czyzowicz2014Evacuating]. Face-to-face, the robots must decide when to look for each other. Czyzowicz et al. obtained a lower bound of $3+\pi/6+\sqrt3 \approx 5.255$ by studying an exit at a vertex of a hexagon, and introduced a "nonintuitive" strategy in which searchers "are forced to detour and meet" [Czyzowicz2020FaceToFace]. Brandt et al. showed that such meetings need not exchange useful information [Brandt2017Collaboration], and Disser and Schmitt brought the upper bound to about $5.6234$ [Disser2019Second]; the gap remains open.

sections.heading: What evacuation varies
sections.body: Each variation changes one ingredient of the original problem. Communication: a sender and a receiver evacuate the disk strictly between the wireless and face-to-face optima [Georgiou2022Asymmetric], and on the line exactly in ratio $3+2\sqrt2$ [Czyzowicz2021GroupEvacuation]. Faults: with one crash-faulty or Byzantine robot among three, the disk bounds are not tight [Czyzowicz2017Faulty]; on the line, evacuation with $k = 2f+1$ robots is a sub-problem of Byzantine search, since all robots may have to reach the target [Czyzowicz2021NearMajority]. Domain: equilateral triangles and squares [Chuangpishit2020Triangles] [Georgiou2026Triangle], $m$ rays [Brandt2020Rays], and disks with two exits [Pattanayak2018TwoExits]. Speeds and energy: two robots with different speeds [Lamprou2020Fast], and the energy spent searching, which Czyzowicz et al. consider "for the first time" [Czyzowicz2019Energy].

sections.heading: Priority evacuation
sections.body: Czyzowicz et al. observe that searchers are usually assumed to have the same capabilities and the same role, yet in practice "only one of the robots has the capability to address an urgent need at the target", such as performing an emergency procedure or closing a breach [Czyzowicz2018Priority]. Priority evacuation makes this the measure: $\sigma$ servants help a distinguished robot, the queen, and only the queen's evacuation time counts [Czyzowicz2018Priority]. For $\sigma$ servants both bounds tend to 2, but they differ in the $1/\sigma$ term [Czyzowicz2018Priority]; for one and two servants, the problem was posed in [Czyzowicz2018GodSaveQueen], and the lower bound for one servant was later raised through weighted group search [Georgiou2025WeightedDisk], leaving a gap between about $4.568$ and $4.819$.

sections.heading: Patrolling
sections.body: Patrolling keeps the geometry and the robots with given maximum speeds but replaces a one-time target by a continuing duty: every point must be visited often enough, and the cost is the idle time, the longest time a point is left unvisited [Kawamura2015Fence]. Kawamura and Kobayashi note that patrolling had been studied mostly through heuristics and experiments, and that theoretical studies "have revealed that there are interesting questions and intricacies even in the simplest settings" [Kawamura2015Fence]. Czyzowicz et al. studied fences patrolled by agents with distinct speeds [Czyzowicz2011Patrolling] and, as Kawamura and Kobayashi report, conjectured that partitioning the fence in proportion to the speeds is always optimal; Kawamura and Kobayashi confirmed this for three agents and disproved it in general [Kawamura2015Fence], and Kawamura and Soejima found schedules that patrol a fence $4/3$ times longer than partition and a circle $21/20$ times better than the simple strategies [Kawamura2020Simple]. Faults enter as in search: with up to $f$ unreliable robots, the optimal idleness of an Eulerian graph is $(f+1)|E|/k$ [Czyzowicz2017Patrolmen]. How far an optimal fence schedule can beat partition remains open [Kawamura2020Simple].
